title: Brace a sagging gate so it holds itself up
instruction: The garden gate has sagged: its latch side has dropped onto the rubber stop. Fit the loose wooden brace between two of the corner seats so that the gate holds itself up, with the top of the latch-side stile no more than 3 mm from level with the top of the hinge-side stile, then let go of the gate and the brace.
context: Hanging and bracing gates is fence and carpentry work (O*NET 47-4031.00, Fence Erectors: "Assemble gates, and fasten gates into position"). A gate brace must run from the bottom of the hinge side to the top of the latch side so the gate's weight puts it in compression; fitted the other way it is in tension and the gate still sags (Jacksons Fencing, "Which way should a garden gate be braced"). A loose brace drops easily onto the wrong diagonal and does nothing, while the right one only goes in after the latch side is lifted square.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Gate frame, standing upright across the table with its face towards the robots: two stiles (green-painted pine, 15 x 20 x 150 mm, 15 mm front to back) and two rails (green-painted pine, 15 x 20 x 220 mm), joined at each corner by a pivot pin running front to back. The pins are 200 mm apart along the rails (at y +10.5 and y -9.5) and at 45 mm and 165 mm above the table, all in the plane x 33. The hinge-side (left, +y) stile is fixed to a wooden post (20 x 20 x 200 mm, standing on the table just behind it) so it stays plumb, its bottom 30 mm above the table. The latch-side (right) stile carries an 80 g steel block (20 x 40 x 20 mm) on its back face and a 12 x 60 x 12 mm wooden handle sticking out to the right from its outer face, 100 mm above the table (when square). It has sagged: its bottom rests on a black rubber stop block (30 x 30 x 16 mm) on the table under it, 14 mm lower than when the frame is square, and the rails slope down to the right. Seats: in each of the frame's four inside corners, a V notch made of two pine plates (35 x 22 x 3 mm, at 90 degrees, opening along the diagonal towards the opposite corner) with a 2 mm back plate, standing 35 mm out from the frame's front face (towards the robots) and fixed to the rail it sits on. Brace: a pine dowel 12 mm across with a 15 mm ball on each end, 183.9 mm between the balls' centres (198.9 mm overall), 30 g, lying on the table along y (left-right) with its centre at x 20, y 0. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured at the end with a steel rule and a photo. 0 unless the brace sits in two diagonally opposite seats (each ball end within 3 mm of its notch's seat point and within the seat's depth), no part of either robot is within 20 mm of the brace, the latch-side stile (with its weight and handle) or either rail, and the latch side moved no more than 0.2 mm over the last second. Then by how far the top of the latch-side stile sits from level with the top of the hinge-side stile: within 3 mm 1.0; within 6 mm 0.5; within 9 mm 0.2; further 0. The trial ends early once the score has been 1.0 for 1 s.
reset_notes: Take the brace out of the seats and lay it back on the table along y, centred at x 20, y 0. The gate drops back onto its stop by itself. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The gate is a pin-jointed parallelogram with light damping and no friction at its pins; the hinge-side stile is fixed, standing for a stile hung on hinges from a fixed post. A real gate's nailed corners resist racking a little on their own; these resist none, so the brace alone holds the gate, and the 80 g weight on the latch side stands in for the leverage of a real gate's own weight. The brace is a loose push-fit member in V-notch seats instead of a brace cut to fit and nailed; it carries the load the same way, in compression on its ends, and cannot pull. Its length is the square frame's seat-to-seat length less 0.8 mm, so seated on the compression diagonal it stops the gate about 1.6 mm below square. Friction 0.6 (gate, brace) and 0.9 (rubber stop).
